children: BlackRock argues that elevated borrowing costs and firm equity markets are not mutually exclusive, even as investors brace for a likely Federal Reserve rate increase on Wednesday.
The firm’s case rests on corporate fundamentals rather than a bet that policy or energy prices will ease quickly. Long-term Treasury yields
have climbed to levels last seen around the 2007 cycle, while Brent crude

has held well above $100 a barrel amid renewed Middle East supply risk, including attacks that have disrupted regional energy infrastructure. Fresh U.S. inflation readings have also pushed markets to treat a quarter-point hike as the base case. Those forces would normally compress equity valuations.

BlackRock says they have not, because expected U.S. earnings have continued to rise. Higher profit forecasts, in the institution’s view, give stocks a buffer against a steeper discount rate and costlier energy inputs. That earnings cushion is why the asset manager is keeping an overweight view in U.S. equities even as the policy and commodity backdrop tightens.

Markets, it argues, are weighing those macro headwinds against still-resilient company results rather than treating higher yields as an automatic sell signal. The implication is that the path of profits, not the level of rates alone, will decide whether stocks can stay constructive after this week’s Fed decision.

title: BlackRock says higher yields and higher stocks can coexist
